explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Matthew says, “…He withdrew to Galilee.” (Matthew 4:12) John, the man who baptized Jesus, has been put in prison, and Jesus heads for Galilee. The text doesn't tell us why, so I won't make something up. I'll just say it's a quiet move, and the big stuff starts right after.

I see why that one tugs at you, friend. John is in prison, so a visit seems like the natural move. But Matthew doesn't say Jesus goes there. It says, “…He withdrew to Galilee.” (Matthew 4:12) That's where He heads.

explanations.answer: He heads back to the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Close, but that's already behind Him, baker. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness, where He fasted forty days and forty nights (Matthew 4:1-2). This time, Matthew says He withdrew to Galilee. I've been stuck in one dusty spot too long myself, so I get the pull to go back. Jesus keeps moving forward.

Capernaum, yes! Matthew says Jesus went and lived there, by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. Notice that He doesn't just pass through. He moves in. A fresh town, a fresh start, and no junk drawer in sight.

Good guess, baker, but Joppa isn't the town Matthew names. He says Jesus left Nazareth and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. Joppa is a different place altogether. I get my cookie shapes mixed up all the time, so no shame here.
Tyre is a real name, friend, but it's not the one on this card. Matthew says Jesus went and lived in Capernaum. That's the town by the sea in Zebulun and Naphtali. Capernaum is the one to hang on to.

Light, baker! Isaiah, the prophet, said, “the people living in darkness have seen a great light…” (Matthew 4:16) Matthew says Jesus moving there fulfills those words. I know a little about living in the dark, and when the light finally showed up in my life, I felt it. Isaiah's words are about that kind of moment.

An army would make a big entrance, I'll give you that. But Isaiah's words say, “the people living in darkness have seen a great light…” (Matthew 4:16) No soldiers in that line at all. Just people in the dark and a light that shows up.

A storm, baker? Too much drama, even for me! The verse says, “the people living in darkness have seen a great light…” (Matthew 4:16) Darkness is in the line, so I see how you got there. But what they see is a light, not a storm.

explanations.answer: They leave their nets at once
explanations.explanation: At once is right, friend. Matthew says, “And at once they left their nets and followed Him.” Simon Peter and Andrew are fishermen, and those nets are their work. When the angel called me out of that drawer, I asked for one minute first, and these two didn't even ask for that.

explanations.answer: They finish the day's catch first
explanations.explanation: That would be the sensible thing, wouldn't it? But the text says, “And at once they left their nets and followed Him.” Nothing in it about finishing the catch. They were casting a net into the sea when Jesus called them, and they left those nets.

explanations.answer: They ask for time to think
explanations.explanation: Most of us would ask, baker. I'd be asking for a calendar and a second opinion. But Matthew says, “And at once they left their nets and followed Him.” There's no time to think in that line.

Zebedee, yes! Matthew says James and his brother John “were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets.” Three of them, one boat, and a whole lot of nets. I'd say that's a family business, and the text puts them all together right there.

Nice try, friend, but Matthew doesn't put an uncle in this boat. He says James and John “were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets.” Zebedee is the name to remember. Alphaeus isn't mentioned in these verses.

Nathanael is a good name, baker, but he's not in this boat. Matthew says James and John “were in a boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets.” Just the two brothers and their father. No Nathanael in these verses.

True, baker. Matthew says, “…immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.” They didn't wait around. Their father Zebedee was right there in the boat with them, and they still went. Matthew doesn't tell us what Zebedee said, so I won't invent a line for him.

This one is true, friend, so False doesn't fit. Matthew says, “…immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.” Jesus called them, and they went right then. Their father Zebedee was in the boat with them, and they left it all behind.

Synagogues, that's it! Matthew says Jesus went throughout Galilee, “teaching in their synagogues…” A synagogue is a place where people gathered, and Jesus taught in them across the whole region. He wasn't staying put in one spot.

Sounds official, I'll give you that. But in this passage, Matthew says Jesus went throughout Galilee, “teaching in their synagogues…” There's no mention of the temple courts here. Synagogues are the answer.
City gates make a good guess, baker. They were busy places. But this verse names a different spot. Jesus went throughout Galilee, “teaching in their synagogues…” That's where Matthew says He taught.

You got it, baker! Matthew says Jesus was “healing every disease and sickness among the people.” Every one. He's teaching, preaching and healing, all in the same trip through Galilee. That's a full day's work, and I'm tired just reading it.

Not this time, friend. Matthew says Jesus went throughout Galilee, “teaching in their synagogues, preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.” Nothing about collecting offerings. Healing is what He's doing.

explanations.answer: Training new teachers of the law
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, baker, since He's teaching. But Matthew doesn't list that here. He says Jesus was “…preaching the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and sickness among the people.” Healing is the answer.

Not quite, baker. Matthew says the large crowds had come “from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.” That's a lot of places on one list. Galilee is only the first one, so the statement is false.

False is right, friend! Matthew says the large crowds followed Him “from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan.” Galilee is just the start of that list. Those crowds came from all over. I've had my cookie boxes drawing a crowd before, but never like that.
